message.content:
Read /tmp/views-tools/BRIEF.md first and follow it (hard rules, base commit, how to test, how to finish).

YOUR PART (LINES): the commands `detail_line` (in `src/views/lines.rs`, with the `line` element's `check` and `element_view`), `join_polyline`, `explode`, `vertex`, `convert_spline`, `offset`, `trim_extend` (in `src/views/lineedit.rs`), and the curve model in `src/views/curves.rs`. curves.rs is shared: dimensions, detail groups, filled regions, make_fill_pattern and EDIT's split/fillet/corner/move/rotate/mirror will use it, so give it a clean public API (a curve from an element's fields and back, the points it is drawn with, bounds, ends, length, nearest point, split, moved/turned/mirrored). Other sub-agents do, in parallel: views, sheets; 3D views, spots; graphics, filters, templates; dimensions; text/tag/linework; regions and groups (they write a little curve code of their own for now). Don't do theirs.

Observed so far (verify; there's much more to find):
- Saved forms: `{"guid","category":"line","view":<view guid>,"style":<line-style guid, Thin Lines by default>,"start":[0.0,0.0],"end":[1000.0,1000.0]}`; a polyline `"points":[[0.0,0.0],[1000.0,0.0],[1000.0,1000.0]],"arcs":[0.0,90.0]`; a circle `"centre":[0.0,0.0],"radius":500.0`; an ellipse `"centre":[0.0,0.0],"radii":[500.0,300.0],"angle":30.0`; `"control":[[0.0,0.0],…]`; `"fit":[[0.0,0.0],…]`; `"start","end","arc":90.0`; a `through` point is saved as `"arc":-123.855026128`; insulation `"insulation":100.0,"points":[…]` (before the curve's fields); a cloud `"cloud":200.0,"revision":"R1","points":[…],"closed":true`. Replies `{"id":…}`. `elements` shows e.g. `"length":1414.21,"level":<level guid>,"shape":"line","style":"Thin Lines"` beside the saved fields.
- Errors: "detail_line: `foo` isn't one of its parameters: view, level, style, insulation, centre_mark, cloud, revision, start, end, through, arc, points, arcs, closed, centre, radius, radii, angle, span, control, knots, fit, start_tangent, end_tangent"; "detail_line: the line: it is 1 mm long or less"; "detail_line: no view named `X`"; a line in the 3D view or a schedule is made then refused by the model check: "line 100013: view3d 100008 isn't a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet". Views by name or id or sheets by number (`common::find_view`); line styles are styles' (`line_style`).
- `/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md` describes the curve model at length (drawn within `FLAT` of the curve; FIT_TOL 0.05 mm; Boehm knot insertion; clamped cubic B-splines with uniform knots unless given; splines through points by distance along them, ends free or along a tangent; 8,192 points cap; 1,000 km reach; revision clouds' scallops; batt insulation): read the paragraphs on detail lines, vertices, insulation, clouds, Offset, Trim/Extend.
- Detail lines in sections, elevations and on sheets (in their own terms); trim_extend's boundary may be a wall's location line or a grid (walls are ARCH's, written in parallel: build inputs with the original; a wall is `{"guid","category":"wall","type","level","start","end","top_level","height","base_offset"}` with an optional `"arc"`); join_polyline's `notes` about dimensions that measured a deleted line (dimensions are another sub-agent's; build inputs with the original).

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).

# Brief for the VIEWS sub-agents (read all of it first)

You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler
written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed
behaviour. Many agents work in parallel, each owning one area. The VIEWS area (views and annotation,
`src/views/`) is owned by the agent that launched you; it split the area between several sub-agents.
Your part is given in your prompt. Do it fully and exactly; don't do the other parts.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it ONLY by running it (args, stdin,
  files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete
  it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Edit only the files your prompt gives you. You may add child modules of your own files
  (`src/views/dims.rs` may say `pub mod geom;` for `src/views/dims/geom.rs`). Do NOT edit
  `src/views/mod.rs`, `src/views/common.rs`, `src/views/model.rs` or anything outside `src/views/`; if you
  need a change there, copy what you need into your own files and say so in your final report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in your own `/tmp/views-<yourpart>/`.
  Commit only Rust (your files). Don't write report/summary .md files into the repo.
- Never use bare `git stash`. Don't push. Don't touch other worktrees or branches but your own.

## Your worktree and base
You run in your own git worktree. FIRST run `git log --oneline -3`: your branch must contain commit
`9de3863` ("Views: the constraints hook…", after "Views: the module's skeleton…"). If it doesn't, run `git merge 9de3863` (or, in a fresh
clean worktree, `git reset --hard 9de3863`). Build with `cargo build --release --offline`
(about 15 s); the binary is `<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`.

## The codebase (read the parts you need)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`; `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps; `Value::f`,
  `Value::u`, `Value::s`; `jobj!{"k" => v, …}`), serde_json-identical parse errors and float
  formatting (`1000.0`, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()`. Command replies are printed
  with keys sorted (as serde_json::Value), so a reply's key order doesn't matter; a saved element's
  field order DOES (match the original's saved files exactly).
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`,
  `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field
  order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}` entries; ids count down from 999999 via
  `alloc_lib_id`, shared with the "parts" elements and types hold, e.g. a region's sketch lines
  `{id, guid, start, end}`, never reused in a session). `alloc_id()` for element ids; `find_guid`,
  `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find(kind,name)`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name(guid)`, `lib_add`. Elements reference each
  other and library entries by GUID (`crate::rand::guid()` makes one).
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command, snapshots the project, runs
  it, then runs `crate::check::check` (which calls every module's `check(pr)`, ours via
  `src/views/mod.rs::check`, which calls your file's `check`), rolls back on any error, and records an
  undo step labelled by the command's catalog label when the project changed (call
  `crate::views::mark_step()` in a command that must make a step even unchanged).
- `src/commands/params.rs`: param readers with the original's texts (`` `x` in mm is required``,
  `` `x` must be a number in mm, got … ``, points, text ≤ 256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9). Many commands have
  texts of their own: always probe.
- `src/model.rs`: levels by elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` with the original's errors (`tag`
  and `dimension` take `level`), `find` by id/GUID, `normalize_guid`, `level_of_view`.
- `src/styles/` (done by another agent): line patterns/styles, fill patterns, filled region types,
  text types, dimension types, line weights, object styles, units, phases, phase filters, design
  options, project parameters. Library kinds: `line-style`, `fill-pattern`, `filled-region-type`,
  `text-type`, `dimension-type`, `view-filter`, `view-template`, `detail-group`, `phase`,
  `phase-filter`, `type:wall`… `styles::common` has colour/pen readers, `check_keys` (the original's
  "`foo` isn't one of its parameters: a, b, c", listing them in the original's order),
  `styles::phasing::check_view_graphics` checks a view's phase/phase filter/options.
- `src/views/` (ours): `mod.rs` dispatches each command to its file's `run(s, cid, p)`, calls each
  file's `check(pr)` after every command, `element_view(pr, id, x)` (what the `elements` command shows
  of an element beyond its saved fields: e.g. a section's `length` and `looking`, a dimension's
  `values` and `labels`, a text's `type` by name and `level`, a line's `shape`, `length`, `style` by
  name; `elements` is done by READERS and calls this hook for our categories), and
  `inspect_entries` (what `inspect` lists of view filters, templates, detail groups).
  `common.rs`: `find_view` / `view_param` (a view by id or name: "`view`: X is not a view", "no view
  named `X`"), `default_plan` (lowest level), `default_3d` / `ensure_default_3d` (the `{3D}` view as
  the original makes it), `r3` (round to the micron, as the original keeps worked-out points),
  `cat_id` ("wall 100002"), field readers, `word(pr, [en, pt, es, sv, cs, fr, nl, de, it])`.
  `model.rs`: a stand-in for model geometry: wall type, thickness, core, location line → centre line
  (exterior face = LEFT of start→end), faces, arc walls (`arc` degrees CCW), base/top heights, plan
  outlines of walls/floors/columns, vector helpers. ARCH and STRUCTURE (walls, doors, floors…, in
  `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`, `src/structure/`) are being written in parallel by others, so the model
  commands (`wall`, `door`, `floor`, `room`, `column`…) do NOT work in our binary yet: write what you need
  of their geometry yourself (in your files), the way the original's saved files and replies show it.

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd]
[-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code,
stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids,

You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.

- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run each command line of a file (or stdin) separately on the original (and optionally mine).
usage: each.py [-m] [-b] [-f in.bimcraft] [-s 'setup cmd']... < cmds.txt
  -m: run mine instead; -b: run both and mark differences; -f: open this project first.
Each line: a command `id {json}` (or several separated by ' ;; ')."""
import os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, re
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ['MINE'] if 'MINE' in os.environ else '/nonexistent-set-MINE'
G = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
a = sys.argv[1:]
exes = [ORIG]
infile = None
setup = []
both = False
while a:
    if a[0] == '-m': exes = [MINE]; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-b': exes = [ORIG, MINE]; both = True; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': infile = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-s': setup.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    else: break
src = open(a[0]) if a else sys.stdin
lines = [l.rstrip('\n') for l in src if l.strip() and not l.startswith('#')]
def norm(s):
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m) + 1)
        return m[g]
    return G.sub(rep, s)
same = 0
for l in lines:
    outs = []
    for exe in exes:
        d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='e', dir=os.environ.get('SCRATCH'))
        args = [exe, 'run']
        if infile:
            shutil.copy(infile, d)
            args.append(os.path.basename(infile))
        for s in setup:
            args += ['--cmd', s]
        for c in l.split(' ;; '):
            args += ['--cmd', c]
        p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
        shutil.rmtree(d)
        o = p.stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip().split('\n')
        o = [x for x in o if x][-1:] if (infile or setup) else o
        outs.append(norm(('OUT ' + '\n    '.join(o) if any(o) else '') + (' ERR ' + p.stderr.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip() if p.stderr else '') + ' [%d]' % p.returncode))
    if both:
        if outs[0] == outs[1]:
            same += 1
            print('SAME', l[:150])
        else:
            print('DIFF', l)
            print('  orig:', outs[0])
            print('  mine:', outs[1])
    else:
        print('>>', l)
        print('  ', outs[0])
if both:
    print('%d/%d same' % (same, len(lines)))
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Probe the original: p.py [-f infile] [-m] -- run args...
Runs in a fresh temp dir; prints stdout/stderr/exit and, for each .bimcraft written,
the elements (and top-level sections that differ from a new project's)."""
import json, os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, re
G=re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ['MINE'] if 'MINE' in os.environ else '/nonexistent-set-MINE'
a = sys.argv[1:]
exe = ORIG
files = []
full = False
while a and a[0] != '--':
    if a[0] == '-m': exe = MINE; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-F': full = True; a = a[1:]
    else: break
if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='p', dir=os.environ.get('SCRATCH'))
for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
p = subprocess.run([exe] + a, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=300)
print('STDOUT:', p.stdout.decode())
print('STDERR:', p.stderr.decode())
print('EXIT:', p.returncode)
base = json.load(open('/tmp/views-tools/new.bimcraft'))
for f in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
    if f.endswith('.bimcraft') and f not in [os.path.basename(x) for x in files]:
        dd = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, f)))
        print('=== file', f)
        for k, v in dd.items():
            if k == 'elements':
                for id, e in v.items():
                    print(' ', id, json.dumps(e, ensure_ascii=False))
            elif k in ('uid', 'library'):
                continue
            elif full or k not in base or G.sub('G',json.dumps(base[k])) != G.sub('G',json.dumps(v)):
                if k in ('format','name','next_id','units','language'):
                    print(' top', k, json.dumps(v))
                else:
                    print(' top', k, json.dumps(v, ensure_ascii=False)[:3000])
        # library entries not in a new project's kinds
        lib = dd.get('library', {})
        bl = {(e['kind'], e['name']) for e in base['library'].values()}
        for id, e in lib.items():
            if (e['kind'], e['name']) not in bl:
                print('  lib', id, json.dumps(e, ensure_ascii=False))
shutil.rmtree(d)

content.content:
Electrical Lighting (outlets hidden) and Electrical Ceiling (the devices that stand on the floor or the wall hidden, luminaires and cable
trays kept). A project from before has none. File format 13 is the one that has these rows: a build that reads up to 12 refuses it on
opening, with an error about a category, not "saved by a newer BIMCraft".

Detail lines and their line styles (`lines.rs`): a `LinePattern` is a freely ordered sequence of 1–32 graphic segments, each length mm
on paper, so it reads the same at any scale (`Solid` is none, a name no pattern takes); a `LineStyle` is a pen, a colour and a
pattern; both are library entries (`Kind::LinePattern`, `Kind::LineStyle`), so a style names its pattern and a detail line its style
by GUID in a file, and a rename (`rename_entry`) follows everywhere. A project starts with ours, named in its language
(`lines::patterns`, `lines::styles`); one in use can't be deleted. A `DetailLine` (category `line`, Lines in Visibility/Graphics) is
drawn in one view, as a text note is: a level's plan (not its ceiling plan), a section or an elevation, or a sheet, in the view's own
terms, and goes with it. `render::detail_line` draws it in its style's pen with the model's line weights, its colour and its
pattern's dashes in pixels at the view's paper (`LinePattern::dash`); a repeat under two pixels draws solid. A primitive's dash is
any list of on and off lengths (`Prim::Line::dash`), which SVG, PDF, the PNG and the canvas all take. The desktop has Annotate >
Detail Line (DL; a line a click, as walls are, chained until Enter or the first point again; the Options Bar's Line Style and
Chain; the Draw panel's other shapes, below) and Manage > Line Styles (`linestyles.rs`: styles and patterns on two tabs of one
draft, applied as one undo step). Patterns > New Pattern or Edit opens the separate Line Pattern Creator
(`linestyles/creator.rs`), with a live straight/curved preview and segment controls, add, reorder and delete. Save Pattern
updates the library draft; Cancel Pattern discards just the creator, and the parent Cancel discards the whole draft.
Segments are Gap (`space`), Straight (`dash`), Dot (`dot_length`, its reserved length, with a circle exactly the pen width),
Offset (`length`, `count` 2–9, `distance` between adjacent lines symmetrically about the centerline), Wave and Zig Zag
(`length`, `frequency` in cycles per segment, `amplitude` from centerline), and Text (`length`, `size`, `text`). Text uses
bundled IBM Plex Sans on Linux, Windows and macOS, with the annotation font fallback for missing characters. Its size is
maximum capital height; it scales uniformly down when its reserved length is shorter than the text. Text is centered on
the axis and each glyph rotates with its own curve tangent. `lines/pattern.rs` makes shared stroke/fill geometry for
preview, canvas, PNG, SVG and PDF; old alternating dash/space/dot patterns retain native dashes. On canvas and paper,
pattern lettering uses the same non-zero contour tessellation as notes, keeping counters transparent during selection
and hover as well as ordinary drawing; dots retain their pen-sized polygon rendering. Tiny or excessively dense
patterns draw solid with bounded work. Region profiles, snapping, alignment and dimensions use the original centerline.
Format 9 adds these segments; older dash/space/dot patterns open unchanged. Next: patterns made from lines drawn in a view.

A detail line and a sketch line are any `curves::Curve`: a polyline (straight segments and arcs, each arc's turn in degrees
counter-clockwise as a wall's; a line or an arc is one of two points), a circle, an ellipse whole or partial, a spline by its
control points (a clamped cubic B-spline, uniform knots unless it holds its own), or a spline through points (a cubic by the
distance along them, each end free or leaving along a tangent). In a file and in a command a curve is flat, the fields of its
shape (`curves::Fields`; `curve_struct!` makes a type that holds one among its own fields, since serde's `flatten` won't take
`deny_unknown_fields`), so an older file's `points` and `closed` read as they did. `Curve::points` draws it with chords no
further than `FLAT` from it; `nearest`, `split`, `map` (a move, a turn or a mirror), `handles` and `moved` (grips) and
`check` are the rest. Splitting is exact but for a spline through points: a polyline's segment or arc divides, an ellipse's
span does, and a control-point spline gets the knot inserted to the degree's multiplicity (Boehm's algorithm) so its halves'
control points are the original's; a spline through points becomes two through the original's points on each side and the
cut, leaving it along the original's tangent, with points of the original added where it strays most until it is within
`FIT_TOL` (QCAD turns the halves into control-point splines instead; Revit won't split a spline at all). A closed curve opens
where it's cut. Commands: `split` (detail lines as walls), `join_polyline` (PJ), `explode` (EX), `fillet` (FL), `corner`
(TR, two detail lines as two walls), `trim_extend` (detail lines to a boundary: Revit's Trim/Extend Single and Multiple
Elements) and `offset` (OF; `draw::offset` keeps arcs concentric and mitres a polyline's corners). `draw::meet` finds where two
lines or arcs cross, run on along their lines or circles, and `draw::trim_to` brings one to it, keeping the part picked.
`draw.rs` is Revit's Draw panel as data: each `Shape` (Line, Rectangle, Inscribed and Circumscribed Polygon, Circle,
Start-End-Radius, Center-ends and Tangent End Arc, Fillet Arc, Spline, Spline Through Points, Ellipse, Partial Ellipse,
Polyline, Pick Lines), how many clicks it takes, what `make` builds from them with the Options Bar's Sides, Radius and Offset,
and the `preview` with the cursor as the next point; `wall_segments` turns lines, arcs and circles into walls and
`element_curve` is what Pick Lines copies. The desktop's `draw.rs` keeps each tool's shape (detail lines, sketches, walls; the
walls' panel offers only lines and arcs), gathers the points in the tool, and makes the lines, sketch lines or walls as one undo
step; Join into Polyline and Explode Polyline sit on Modify | Lines and work on picked sketch lines too. A detail line
selected alone shows its handles as grips (corners, control points, points passed through, a circle's or an ellipse's centre;
a spline's frame dashed), dragged and snapped, then `modify` with the moved curve's fields (the other shapes' set to null).
Modify's Split, Trim/Extend to Corner, Trim/Extend Single and Multiple Elements and Offset take detail lines as they take
walls, and while sketching they change the sketch's lines (`sketch_modify`).

Vertices come and go (`vertex`; Modify | Lines' Add Vertex and Delete Vertex, on sketch lines too): `Curve::with_vertex`
cuts a polyline's segment, inserts a knot in a control-point spline (one control point more, the curve exactly as it was)
or a point in a spline through points; `without_vertex` takes a corner, a control point or a point out. `convert_spline`
(Convert Spline) turns a spline through points into the same curve by control points, exactly (`fit_to_control`: knots at
the points' distances along, a tridiagonal system for the control points with the fitted spline's end conditions), and
one by control points into one through points within `FIT_TOL` (`refit_with`); Revit converts neither way.

Revit's Insulation is a detail line with an `insulation` width: `DetailLine::drawn` gives `lines::batt`, a prolate cycloid
along its curve (loops the whole width across, `BULGE` times it apart), so it splits, offsets, joins and takes grips as any
line does, and follows arcs and splines, which Revit's doesn't. Annotate > Detail > Insulation draws it, its Width on the
Options Bar; Properties shows Insulation Width. A revision cloud is the same idea: a detail line with a `cloud` arc length (and
a `revision`, any text) that `drawn` turns into scallops (`lines::cloud`, arcs of `SCALLOP` degrees bulging out of a loop
whichever way round it was drawn, to the left of an open line). A scallop ends at each corner where the way turns by more
than about 25 degrees (so a rectangle's scallops never cut a corner) and, past 1,024 scallops or more corners than that
allows, the scallops are even and fewer, each drawn within its share of `MAX_DRAWN` points. A line is a cloud or insulation
(`DetailLine::check` refuses both). `revision` is a label: it is kept with the cloud and `elements` lists it, and no
schedule reads it yet. Annotate > Detail > Revision Cloud draws one, a rectangle by
default; with it a rectangle or a polygon is one cloud round (`curves::join`), and Line is one cloud through the points
(`one_line`). `centre_mark` is Revit's Center Mark Visible: a 3 mm cross at each of `Curve::centres`, the Options Bar's Show
Centre for new arcs and circles.

Linework (`linework`, LW) is Revit's: an edge of a model element drawn in a line style in one plan, or hidden there. The
plan's `Graphics::linework` holds each as the element's GUID, the edge's two ends and a style (`None` hidden).
`render::edge_at` finds the edge picked: the plan drawn again around the point without its linework, the nearest
segment of the element's lines within `LINEWORK_REACH`. `render::linework` restyles, after `Look::dress`, the parts of the
element's lines that lie along that edge (collinear within a pixel, over its length), so one face of a wall changes and the
rest of its outline doesn't. Picked again, an edge's entry is replaced; `remove` takes out the one nearest the point (the desktop's
`<By Category>`), not every edge within reach: both faces of a thin wall are. An entry on an edge the element no longer draws (a
wall across a styled face cut it in two) is stale: the drawing still restyles what it overlaps, and where the edge picked has
no entry, `remove` takes the nearest stale entry within `LINEWORK_REACH`, one a call, never one on another edge that is
drawn (`render::edges_at` lists the edges drawn). A view's linework is checked (`Graphics::check`):
at most `MAX_LINEWORK` (2,000) edges, ends within `MAX_COORD`, and a line style the project has. The drawing splits an element's
lines along all its edges in one pass (`render::linework`: the cost is the prims plus the edges, not a pass over every prim for

content.content:
lines along all its edges in one pass (`render::linework`: the cost is the prims plus the edges, not a pass over every prim for
each edge). A line style a view's linework uses can't be deleted, and an element's entries go with it.

Text notes and text types (`text.rs`). A `Note` is drawn in one view, as a detail line is, and is of a text type
(`Model::text_types`, library entries of `Kind::TextType`, so a file names a note's type by GUID and `rename_entry` follows a
rename): Revit's font, size (its capitals' height on paper, mm), bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour, and a border
`border_offset` mm on paper round its text in pen `border_pen`, from whose side nearer its end a leader starts. A project starts
with 2.5mm, 3.5mm and 5mm in Arial; `text_type` makes, renames and deletes them (none in use). A type's font is a name:
any font the system has, or one we carry (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, BIMCraft Lettering: `font.rs`'s single-stroke
capitals). `text/system.rs` lists the system's fonts once (`system::index`): it looks through the folders Linux, Windows
and macOS keep them in and reads each file only as far as its OpenType table directory and its `name`, `OS/2` and `head`
tables (family, weight, italic, whether it varies its weight), from the public specification, every offset checked; a face
is read whole (`system::load`, kept, up to `MAX_FONT`) only when a note is lettered in it. `text::resolve` turns a type's font
and a character's bold and italic into a `Face`: ours by name; else the family; else its stand-ins (`system::substitutes`:
Arial by Liberation Sans, Arimo, Helvetica, Nimbus Sans, DejaVu Sans…, Times New Roman and Courier New likewise); else Plex
Sans. So Arial, the default, letters on any system, and a file naming a font this one hasn't opens (`TextType::check`
takes any name) and draws with what stands in; the `text_type` command refuses a font the system can't letter, unless the
type has it already. A family's own bold and italic faces are taken where it has them; else a variable face is set to
`wght` 700, any other is made bold by its outline drawn round heavier (our lettering by heavier strokes), and italic by
slanting it. A character a face hasn't is lettered from Plex Sans, then Plex Mono, then the system's wide fonts
(`system::FALLBACKS`: Noto Sans CJK, Microsoft YaHei, PingFang…), else drawn as the lettering's question mark.
`text::shape` reads a glyph's outline with `ttf-parser` once and keeps it. `text_type` without a name lists the fonts
(`text::families`) and what letters each type here (`drawn_with`); Type Properties shows "drawn with" when that differs. A note may override bold, italic and underline on parts of itself: `override_format`
lets its `runs` (character ranges, a line break one character) count, each setting any of the three either way, so a part
stays bold, or not, whatever type the note gets. `modify` with new `text` alone keeps the runs on what didn't change
(`text::remap`: the common start and end keep theirs, what came in takes the format before it). `text::layout` lays a note out
in mm on paper (lines `LINE_PITCH` sizes apart, each character's place and width), which `render::note` draws (each letter a
`Prim::Fill` of rings filled by the non-zero rule, our lettering and Plex Mono's bold as lines, underlines as lines; `Part::Text`)
and which the desktop's editor reads for its caret, its selection and a click's place (`Layout::caret`, `boxes`, `index_at`;
`Drawing::note_frame` turns layout mm into the drawing's pixels and back). The canvas fills a letter, holes and all, from
`text::triangles` (strips between every corner's and crossing's height), kept by its points for the frames that draw it again.
A file of format 7 has notes with a `size`: reading it gives each a type of that size (`Model::typed_notes`), and `Model::check`
refuses a `size` left on one. A note holds up to `MAX_NOTE` (4,000) characters and `MAX_RUNS` (1,000) runs.

Detail groups (`groups.rs`) are Revit's: `create_group` (GP) makes the detail lines, filled regions and text notes given,
all of one view, into a group type (`Model::detail_groups`) holding them as `Member`s about the middle of them, in no
view, and puts one `DetailGroup` element in their place. Members are parts (`HasPart`, `parts_now`): each has its own id
and GUID, and their line styles and region types are library references like an element's (`lib_refs_mut`), so renames
reach them; `Model::check` holds each to what the same element in a view must be (`annotation_ok`). A placed group is an
origin, an angle and `mirrored`; `groups::placed` gives its members as elements of its view (through
`commands::transform`, as Move and Rotate take elements), which `render::detail_group` draws, regions under lines and notes,
all owned by the group, so it picks, moves, rotates and mirrors as one. `ungroup` (UG) puts those elements back in the view;
`group_type` renames a type (its groups follow) or deletes it while nothing is of it. A `RepeatingDetail` places a group
along a line every `spacing` from its start, each turned along it (at most `MAX_REPEATS`), as Revit's Repeating Detail
Component does with a detail component. A view draws every member of every group and repeat in it each time, so
`Model::check` caps what one view places: a group counts its type's members, a repeating detail its members once for each
repeat, and `MAX_PLACED` (10,000) is the most in a view (measured with the probe `probe_the_cost_of_the_most_hatched_regions_a_view_may_place`,
10,000 hatched regions take about 0.1 s to draw at 3 m across and 0.5 s at 30 m across, 2.8 million primitives, on a machine that
is not busy, in a dev build (the core is built at opt-level 2 there) and in release alike, and up to 0.29 s and 1.10 s in the dev
build on a busy one; the 200,000 it once allowed took 6 s and 30 million primitives). A placed member that is a huge circle costs
more (the probe `probe_the_cost_of_placed_members_that_are_huge_circles`: 8,192 points each, about 0.2 ms to draw and 3 to 5 ms to
rasterize, 8 ms on a busy machine), so a view at the cap of them can take a minute or more to render; the cap stays. A member note keeps its own angle under a pure mirror
(it still reads the right way round) and turns with the group's angle. The file holds a group's members as elements, and
`Model::read` leaves out of them what this build doesn't know, as it does for any element
(`/detail_groups/<name>/members/<i>/element/...`). Deleting a line style that a filled region or a group's member is drawn in
is refused with the region's or the group's name. On the desktop, Annotate > Detail has Detail Group, Repeating Detail and
Create Group, and the right-click menu has Create Group and Ungroup.

A project with any of this (line styles and patterns, fill patterns, region types, detail lines, regions, groups, repeating
details, sketches) needs file format 6, and every file is saved as 6 now, with or without any of it: a build that reads up to 5
would fail on one with a serde error, so 6 makes it say that the file is from a newer BIMCraft (even for a plain project). Nothing
in a file of 5 changes, so `Model::migrate` has no step for 5 to 6.

The Options Bar's Offset puts a line, an arc or a polyline beside the points clicked; a rectangle, a polygon or a circle grows
by it as a whole (`grown`, its corners joined), and a spline or an ellipse takes none (`Shape::offsets`). Modify's Offset takes
ellipses and splines too, as a spline through points within `FIT_TOL` of the true offset (`curves::offset_fit`), refused where
it would fold over itself. While a shape is drawn its numbers can be typed (`draw::numbers`, `reading`, `typed`): a rectangle's
width and height (Tab between them, the canvas taking the Tab from egui's focus), a circle's or a polygon's radius, the third
point's radius, angle or reach; anything else typed is a length toward the cursor, as a line's, in sketch mode too. The canvas
labels them as they read (`shape_dimensions`). A spline or a polyline finishes with Enter, a double click or the right-click
menu's Finish Drawing; Fillet Arc previews the arc nearest the cursor and its radius, Offset a dashed ghost of the copy, and
Trim/Extend and Fillet's picks so far show in the selection's colour. Trim/Extend to Corner with two lines or walls selected (or
two sketch lines picked) joins them at once, each keeping the part toward its middle.

`Drawing::detail` is the level the plan or the section is drawn at: coarse leaves out a compound element's layers and an opening's
symbols, medium its patterns (`cut_layer`, a floor's `surface`), fine draws as before. In the 3D view `Look::style` picks how
`Scene::picture` draws: shaded as ever, hidden line as a section's picture is (paper faces, edges), wireframe by `Scene::edges` (where
surfaces meet at an angle or end, found once) drawn through the faces; a pixel within two of a line picks its element.

A view's graphics (`graphics.rs`; `Level`, `Section` and `View3D` each hold `graphics`) hide and override by category, by view
filter (`Model::view_filters`: categories and a schedule filter's rules, `schedule::picks`) and by element: an element's own beats
the filters' (the first applied prevailing), which beat the category's, and hiding by any of them hides. `Look::of` resolves a
view to what it hides and how it paints the rest; the drawing code asks `look.shows(id)` wherever it loops over elements (plans,
sections, `cut_outlines`, `seen_below`, `view3d::Scene::picture`) and `look.dress` recolours the finished `Drawing` by owner and
by `Part` (`Drawing::part` marks what is drawn as projection, cut, lettering or hatching (and the lines between layers), so a
new drawing of what a view cuts sets `Part::Cut`; a hidden door's opening is drawn owned by none, the wall's; the cut walls' union fill has no owner and takes its colour at the draw site, `cut_unions`). A view template
(`Model::view_templates`), for a kind of view (`ViewKind`: plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; `from` sets it, none is any),
controls groups of the views that follow it (categories, filters, a plan's view range through
`Model::view_range_of`, a phase with its phase filter, design options, scale, detail level, visual style), and they can't change those
(`graphics`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style` and `modify` refuse). Snaps, Tag All, the desktop's Select All
Instances and the framing of sections and 3D views take what `Look` shows too. A level's ceiling plan is its plan's view;
transparency shows in 3D only. A surface is seen through as much as the greater of its material's `transparency` (`Tri::alpha`, in
plain views too) and the view's override for its element (not in a plain view); both painters take it from `Tri::alpha`.

A 3D view sketches on its work plane (`workplane.rs`), as Revit's Work Plane > Set and more: `View3D::work_plane`, a `WorkPlane` on a
`level` (a GUID, in `visit_refs!`), through three `points`, or on a `surface` picked on the model (a point and a normal), each moved
`offset` mm along its normal; with none, the lowest level (`Model::work_plane`). `WorkPlane::resolve` gives it as a `workplane::Frame`,
a point and a unit normal, at any angle, upright too: three points along a line are refused (`workplane::through`, facing up unless
upright), and `Model::check` resolves it. `Frame::over_plan` is it as a `walls::Plane` over the plan, as a floor's top is, for a sketch
that stays plan lines raised onto it (none for an upright one); `Frame::axes` are its level and up directions. The `work_plane` command
sets it (making the default 3D view, as `section_box` does), moves the plane as it is given only `offset`, or, given nothing, clears it;

229:| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
230:| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
231:| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
233:| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
234:| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
235:| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
248:| Annotation | Aligned dimensions between parallel references, one segment or a chain: wall faces, centre lines and ends, door and window centres and jambs, grids; and between endpoints (a wall's ends and its faces' corners, a line's or a grid's ends, a jamb's), aligned along them or linear, horizontal or vertical, as the cursor lies or the Options Bar says (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them); angular dimensions between two lines that meet, radial and diameter ones on round columns, curved walls, circles and arcs, and arc length ones along a curved wall or an arc; all measuring the model as it is, so they follow what they measure (a change that would turn a reference out of parallel with the others is refused). In a 3D view, aligned dimensions between two points or edges of the model (square to an edge), kept by the view and drawn over it, on either painter and on the sheets that hold it. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. Dimension types, as Revit's type parameters: continuous, baseline or ordinate strings, diagonal, arrow, open arrow or dot ticks, pens, colour, the dimension and witness lines' extensions, gaps and control, and the numbers' font, size, lettering, offset, background, read convention, units and rounding; a dimension's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display (EQ). Tags on any element showing its type, a door's or window's mark, a room's name or any field of its schedule, going where their doors and windows go, with or without a leader; tag everything not tagged yet in one go. Text notes in plans, sections, elevations and on sheets, at any angle, over several lines, with a leader, of a text type (font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour and a border: any font the system has, Arial by default, which a look-alike such as Liberation Sans stands in for where it isn't installed, or IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono or our single-stroke lettering; any script a font on the system has, CJK included), written and rewritten on the canvas (Shift+Enter breaks a line), and with Override Formatting, parts of them bold, italic or underlined whatever their type; spot elevations reading the top of what they stand on in plan (a floor, a roof's slope, a stair's tread), or the height of a point in a section |
265:| Desktop | Revit's layout: ribbon tabs with a contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Type Properties, the Project Browser and views in tabs; a plan and a reflected ceiling plan per level that pan and zoom, sections and elevations, a 3D view that orbits, and sheets; tools for walls (straight or arcs, on the location line picked), doors, windows, columns, roofs by footprint (and Gable Edge, to stand a roof's edge upright) and by extrusion, dormers, floors (and a floor's slope arrow), ceilings, shaft openings, sketch mode (Edit Boundary on a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft, and Boundary Line or Sketch Ceiling for a new one: lines, rectangles, arcs and Pick Walls, sketch lines with ids of their own picked by click or box and moved by their grips, Finish Edit Mode saying what's wrong and marking the lines; in the 3D view, Edit Boundary sketches on the element's own plane, and Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft sketch on the view's Work Plane: a level from the list, a surface or three points picked on the model (snapping to corners), each with an offset, at any angle; walls, beams and braces, columns and structural columns, footings, pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays and components draw in the 3D view on the level face under the cursor, snapping as a plan does, a run climbing from one face to another; they need it horizontal), masses (and floors, walls and roofs from them), stairs and ramps (run by run, turning at landings), railings, rooms, levels, grids, dimensions (aligned, angular, radial), spot elevations, text, detail lines, filled and masking regions, tags, sections and elevations; Flip, Attach Top/Base and Detach Top/Base for walls; a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's layers in Type Properties, and the project's materials in Manage > Materials; project parameters in Manage > Project Parameters, and their values in Properties; schedules from View > Schedules, their fields, filters, sorting and totals in Schedule Properties; the Component tool, families and their types in the Type Selector, the Project Browser and Type Properties, a component's own parameters in Properties, and Load Family; Crop View with grips to drag a crop region's edges, and the view range in Properties; project units, metric or feet and inches; Revit's selection (click, Ctrl, Shift, Tab, window and crossing boxes); dragging and the Modify panel (Align, Offset, Mirror, Split, Move, Copy, Rotate, Trim/Extend to Corner) and its Phasing panel (Demolish); Paint and Remove Paint on its Geometry panel, for the 3D view; typed lengths and temporary dimensions; undo and redo; open, save and export; a light and a dark theme; English, Portuguese or Spanish. The Manage tab has the Materials window (with textures and pictures), the Favorites, Object Styles, Annotation Settings (Line Weights, Line Styles, Line Patterns and Fill Patterns, a fill pattern simple or made of detail lines picked in a plan and the tile between two corners), and the Family Editor (New Family, Edit Family) |
376:| Align, trim, split, offset | Align (AL): hover to highlight an edge or centre line, pick the reference, then the target edge. It turns and moves walls, columns, components, slabs, roofs, structural/MEP runs and detail geometry onto the reference in one undo step; hosted doors and windows slide along their wall. While sketching, align sketch lines to model edges or other sketch lines; joined endpoints follow, with sketch undo until Finish. Trim/Extend to Corner (TR): pick two walls on the parts to keep. Split Element (SL): click a wall where to cut it. Offset (OF): point to a wall, and a copy goes to the cursor's side at the Options Bar's distance |
398:| Materials | Manage > Materials: the project's library. Pick a material, or New for another, and set its name, colour, cut pattern and surface pattern; Delete takes one out that no layer uses. A layer picks its material from the library. Texture picks a pattern drawn in code, or Picture… a PNG or JPEG file from your disk, for the 3D view; its tile's width and height, angle and offset follow; Save to Favorites keeps the material, and Favorites… opens them |
480:| `door` | DR | `at`, or `wall` and `offset?`; `type?`, `family?` (a door family's `type`, its first by default), `mark?`, `flip_facing?`, `flip_hand?` |
484:| `floor` | | `boundary?` (else the walls of the level) or `sketch?` (lines, in any order, solved into its outline and openings), `openings?` (holes in it, inside it and apart; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it), `level?`, `type?`, `offset?` (its top above the level), `slope?` (degrees) and `arrow?` (its tail and head: it rises from the tail toward the head), `structural?` (a floor that carries load, as Revit's Floor: Structural). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof`, `shaft`, `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` hold to it too, saying which edges); a saved file that has one still opens. Its model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (set with `modify`) |
485:| `ceiling` | | `point` (in a room: out to its walls' faces, open round the walls standing free inside it), `boundary` or `sketch`, `openings?` (holes in it, inside it and apart), `level?`, `type?`, `offset?` (its underside above the level, 2600) |
496:| `footing` | FI | `at`, `type?`, `thickness?` (400), `offset?` (its top over the level, 0), `angle?`, `level?`: an isolated footing |
497:| `beam` | BM | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (the height of its `justify` line over the level at its start, 0), `end_offset?` (at its end, for one segment: it slopes), `justify?` (`top`, `centre`, `bottom`), `system?`: a beam for each segment |
498:| `pipe` | PI | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (the height of its `justify` line over the level at its start, 0), `end_offset?` (at its end, for one segment: it falls or rises, or stands if the two points are one), `justify?` (`centre` by default), `system?`: a pipe for each segment |
503:| `ground_conductor` | GC | as `pipe`: an earthing conductor (the ring or mesh), usually under the level (a negative `offset`) |
505:| `strip_footing` | FW | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (its top over the level, 0), `system?`: a footing under a wall for each segment |
509:| `roof` | | `level?` (the one above the lowest), `offset?`, `boundary?` (else the walls of the level below) or `sketch?` (its outline and courtyards), `courtyards?` (holes in it with eaves of their own, inside it and apart; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it), `overhang?`, `slope?` (0 is flat), `slopes?` (a slope in degrees for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for the roof's `slope`), `gables?` (edges left upright, edge i from point i to the next, a courtyard's numbered on after the boundary's), `gable?` (a rectangle's short ends), `extrusion?` (`line`, `profile` of `[along, up]` points, `from?`, `to`: swept across to the line's left), `openings?`, `join?` (a roof it ends against), `type?` |
515:| `tag` | TG | `ids?` (without them, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`), `label?` (the field it shows: any of its category's schedule fields), `level?`, `category?`, `offset?`, `leader?` |
541:| `line_pattern` | | `name?`, `segments?` (1–32 freely ordered Gap/`space`, Straight/`dash`, `dot_length`, `offset`, `wave`, `zigzag`, `text` segments; lengths in paper mm), `rename?`, `delete?`: create/edit a graphic line pattern. Offset has `length`, `count` (2–9), `distance`; waves/zigzags have `length`, `frequency` (cycles per segment), `amplitude`; text has `length`, `size`, `text`, in bundled IBM Plex Sans, flowing along curves. Geometry and dimensions retain the centerline. Without a name, lists every pattern |
548:| `detail_line` | DL | a curve: `points` ([[x, y], …], with `arcs` and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` or `through`), `centre` and `radius`, `centre` and `radii` (with `angle` and `span`), `control` (with `knots`) or `fit` (with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`); `view?` (a level's plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet: in its own terms), `style?` (Thin Lines), `insulation?` (a width: batt insulation along it), `cloud?` (an arc length: a revision cloud along it) with `revision?` (its label), `centre_mark?`: a line, arc, polyline, circle, ellipse or spline drawn in one view only, in a line style (Thin Lines by the project's language). An arc, circle or ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin, and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm |
549:| `join_polyline` | PJ | `ids`: detail lines meeting end to end joined into one polyline |
556:| `explode` | EX | `id`: a polyline taken apart into lines and arcs (Revit has no shortcut; PX is the desktop's Plumbing Fixture) |
557:| `vertex` | | `id`, `at`, `delete?`: a vertex more (or fewer) in a polyline or a spline; a control point added keeps the curve |
558:| `convert_spline` | | `id`: a spline through points to the same curve by control points, or back within 0.05 mm |
559:| `fillet` | FL | `ids` (two straight detail lines, or two walls), `radius`: the corner rounded by an arc, the lines cut back to it (a wall's doors and windows stay where they stand in plan, as in `corner`, and only their offset along the wall changes) |
564:| `point_cloud` | | `path` (a PTS, XYZ, PLY, LAS or E57 scan, or a list of a survey's station files) or `cloud` (one the project holds), `name?`, `level?`, `at?`, `offset?`, `angle?`, `units?` (`m` by default), `spacing?` (one point in each cube that wide), `origin?` (`centre`, its middle on `at` and its foot on the level; or `file`, where its coordinates put it). Drawn in the 3D view, plans and sections, snapped to in plans; IFC export leaves it out |
567:| `component` | CM | `family`, `type?` (its first), `at`, `level?`, `angle?`, `offset?`, `mirrored?`, `params?` {parameter: value}: a family's type placed |
570:| `material` | | `name`, `color?` (`#rrggbb` or `[r, g, b]`), `cut?` and `surface?` (`none`, `solid`, `diagonal`, `crosshatch`, `horizontal`, `vertical`, `grid`, `brick`, `concrete`, `insulation`), `texture?` ({`kind?` (`brick`, `block`, `boards`, `concrete`, `plaster`, `tile`, `roof`, `fabric`, `metal`, `insulation` or `image`), `size?` [width, height] mm, `angle?`, `offset?` [x, y], `path?` (a PNG or JPEG file taken into the project), `image?` (a picture's id)}, or null), `rename?`, `delete?`: a material of the project's library, created or changed; layers pick theirs from it |
580:| `trim_extend` | | `boundary` (a detail line, a wall or a grid), `ids` (detail lines of the boundary's view), `keep` (a point on each): each trimmed or extended to the boundary |
581:| `offset` | OF | `id` (a detail line), `distance`, `toward` (a point on the side), `copy?` (true): the line drawn again beside itself, arcs round the same centres; a polyline moves each side and makes its corners where the moved sides meet |

"""lens.py file: each line a detail_line param JSON; prints the length `elements` shows for each (one run)."""
import subprocess, sys, json, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
lines = [l.strip() for l in open(sys.argv[1]) if l.strip() and not l.startswith('#')]
exe = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else ORIG
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='l', dir='/tmp/views-lines/scratch')
args = [exe, 'run']
for l in lines:
    args += ['--cmd', 'detail_line ' + l]
args += ['--cmd', 'elements {"category":"line"}']
p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=600)
shutil.rmtree(d)
out = p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')
if p.returncode != 0:
    print(p.stderr.decode())
els = json.loads(out[-1])['elements']
for l, e in zip(lines, els):
    print(e.get('length'), e.get('shape'), l)

dimension | Aligned Dimension | {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm. It follows what it measures

modify | Modify | {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

move | Move | {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall moves

copy | Copy | {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

rotate | Rotate | {ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

mirror | Mirror | {ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

corner | Trim/Extend to Corner | {ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep

fillet | Fillet Arc | {ids: [a, b], radius} rounds the corner where two straight detail lines, or two straight walls, meet (or would, extended) with an arc of `radius` mm, in the first's line style or of the first's type: each is cut back to the arc

delete | Delete | {ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted

import math
def ell_pts(c, a, b, ang, t0, sw, N):
    ca, sa = math.cos(math.radians(ang)), math.sin(math.radians(ang))
    out = []
    for i in range(N+1):
        t = t0 + sw*i/N
        x, y = a*math.cos(t), b*math.sin(t)
        out.append((c[0] + x*ca - y*sa, c[1] + x*sa + y*ca, t))
    return out
def nearest(pts, at):
    best = None
    for i in range(len(pts)-1):
        p, q = pts[i], pts[i+1]
        dx, dy = q[0]-p[0], q[1]-p[1]
        L2 = dx*dx+dy*dy
        s = ((at[0]-p[0])*dx + (at[1]-p[1])*dy)/L2 if L2 > 0 else 0
        s = max(0.0, min(1.0, s))
        x, y = p[0]+s*dx, p[1]+s*dy
        d = math.hypot(at[0]-x, at[1]-y)
        if best is None or d < best[0]:
            best = (d, i, s)
    d, i, s = best
    t = pts[i][2] + s*(pts[i+1][2]-pts[i][2])
    return t, i, s
for at, want in [((500,0), 320.9101819870768), ((0,300), 71.91495077951168)]:
    for N in range(140, 300):
        pts = ell_pts((0,0), 500, 300, 30, 0.0, 2*math.pi, N)
        t, i, s = nearest(pts, at)
        deg = math.degrees(t)
        if abs(deg - want) < 1e-6:
            print(at, N, repr(deg), want)

    # variant: h via sqrt(r^2 - (c/2)^2)
    h2 = math.sqrt(max(0, r*r - (c/2)**2)) * (1 if abs(t) < math.pi else -1)

def arc_geo(a, b, deg):
    t = math.radians(deg)
    c = math.hypot(b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])
    r = c/(2*abs(math.sin(t/2)))
    m = ((a[0]+b[0])/2, (a[1]+b[1])/2)
    h = r*math.cos(t/2)
    dx, dy = b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]; l = math.hypot(dx, dy); n = (-dy/l, dx/l)
    s = 1.0 if t > 0 else -1.0
    cen = (m[0]+n[0]*h*s, m[1]+n[1]*h*s)
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1]-cen[1], a[0]-cen[0])
    return cen, r, a0, t
for a, b, deg, at in [((0.0,0.0),(200.0,0.0),90.0,(100.0,-35.0)), ((0.0,0.0),(200.0,0.0),40.0,(80.0,-10.0)), ((0.0,0.0),(20.0,0.0),180.0,(5.0,-5.0)), ((0.0,0.0),(2000.0,0.0),20.0,(700.0,-150.0))]:

import math
def geo(a, b, deg):
    t = math.radians(deg)
    c = math.hypot(b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1])
    r = c/(2*abs(math.sin(t/2)))
    m = ((a[0]+b[0])/2, (a[1]+b[1])/2)
    h = r*math.cos(t/2)
    dx, dy = b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]; l = math.hypot(dx, dy); n = (-dy/l, dx/l)
    s = 1.0 if t > 0 else -1.0
    cen = (m[0]+n[0]*h*s, m[1]+n[1]*h*s)
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1]-cen[1], a[0]-cen[0])
    return cen, r, a0, t
def line_circle(a, b, c, r):
    d = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]); l = math.hypot(*d); d = (d[0]/l, d[1]/l)
    f = (a[0]-c[0], a[1]-c[1])
    along = -(f[0]*d[0] + f[1]*d[1])

    l = math.hypot(*v); k = 1.0/l; return (v[0]*k, v[1]*k)

import math
def find_span(knots, p, n, u):
    if u >= knots[n]:
        k = n - 1
        while k > p and knots[k] == knots[k+1]: k -= 1
        return k
    lo, hi = p, n
    mid = (lo+hi)//2
    while u < knots[mid] or u >= knots[mid+1]:
        if u < knots[mid]: hi = mid
        else: lo = mid
        mid = (lo+hi)//2
    return mid
def basis_funs(i, u, p, U):
    """NURBS book A2.2"""
    N = [0.0]*(p+1); left = [0.0]*(p+1); right = [0.0]*(p+1)
    N[0] = 1.0
    for j in range(1, p+1):
        left[j] = u - U[i+1-j]
        right[j] = U[i+j] - u
        saved = 0.0
        for r in range(j):
            temp = N[r]/(right[r+1] + left[j-r])
            N[r] = saved + right[r+1]*temp
            saved = left[j-r]*temp
        N[j] = saved
    return N
def curve_point(P, U, p, u):
    n = len(P)
    span = find_span(U, p, n, u)
    N = basis_funs(span, u, p, U)
    x = 0.0; y = 0.0
    for j in range(p+1):
        x += N[j]*P[span-p+j][0]
        y += N[j]*P[span-p+j][1]
    return (x, y)
def curve_point2(P, U, p, u):
    # accumulate as point = point + N*P (vector style)
    n = len(P)
    span = find_span(U, p, n, u)
    N = basis_funs(span, u, p, U)
    c = [0.0, 0.0]
    for j in range(p+1):
        q = P[span-p+j]
        c = [c[0] + q[0]*N[j], c[1] + q[1]*N[j]]
    return tuple(c)

from refit3 import fit_to_control, drawn, poly_dist, un3, rr
from bspl3 import deboor_v
from bspl import default_knots, degree_of
from refit import orig
def refit(C, u0, u1, init_u, tol, cap, N=256, h=1e-6):
    us = sorted(set([u0 + (u1-u0)*k/N for k in range(N+1)] + list(init_u)))
    S = [C(u) for u in us]
    M = len(us) - 1
    a, b = C(u0), C(u0 + h*(u1-u0)); st = un3((b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]))
    a, b = C(u1 - h*(u1-u0)), C(u1); et = un3((b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1]))
    chosen = sorted(set([0, M] + [us.index(u) for u in init_u]))
    picks = 0
    while picks < cap:
        Q = [[rr(S[i][0]), rr(S[i][1])] for i in chosen]
        P, kn = fit_to_control(Q, st, et)
        D = drawn(P, kn, 3)
        worst = None
        for k in range(M+1):
            if k in chosen: continue
            d = poly_dist(D, S[k])
            if worst is None or d > worst[0]: worst = (d, k)
        if worst is None or worst[0] <= tol: break
        chosen.append(worst[1]); chosen.sort(); picks += 1
    return [(rr(S[i][0]) + 0.0, rr(S[i][1]) + 0.0) for i in chosen]

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""chk2.py base.bimcraft cases.txt: like chk.py but saves after `grid` and prints the modified line as saved."""
import json, sys, subprocess, tempfile, shutil, os
base = sys.argv[1]
for l in open(sys.argv[2]):
    l = l.strip()
    if not l or l.startswith('#'): continue
    eid, upd = l.split(' ', 1)
    upd = json.loads(upd)
    d = json.load(open(base))
    e = d['elements'][eid]
    for k, v in upd.items():
        if v is None: e.pop(k, None)
        else: e[k] = v
    t = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='c', dir='/tmp/views-lines/scratch')
    open(os.path.join(t, 'in.bimcraft'), 'w').write(json.dumps(d, indent=2))
    p = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable', 'run', 'in.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'grid {"start":[0,0],"end":[0,5000]}', '--save', 'o.bimcraft'], cwd=t, capture_output=True)
    print('>>', l)
    if p.returncode == 0:
        o = json.load(open(os.path.join(t, 'o.bimcraft')))['elements'][eid]
        print('  ', json.dumps(o))
    else:
        print('  ', p.stderr.decode().strip())
    shutil.rmtree(t)
